content.title: About
content.content: Pork skin rinds (also known as pork cracklings, chicharrones, or pork chips) are dried and fried pieces of pig skin, often seasoned with salt, spices, or flavorings. They have a crunchy texture and a rich, meaty flavor. The snack is popular in many cuisines worldwide, especially in the United States where it is called pork rinds.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional preparation methods date back to Latin American and Caribbean cuisines.
In the US pork rinds are often marketed as a low‑carb snack for keto diets.
Classic cooking involves boiling the skin first, then deep‑frying it until golden and crisp.
Sweet versions exist, coated with caramel or honey.
In some regions the skins are used as a base for soups and broths.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork rinds contain about 60 % protein, making them a substantial source of amino acids for low‑carb eaters.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: They contain virtually no carbs, which suits keto and paleo dietary patterns.

items.title: Contains collagen
items.content: Collagen from the skin may support joint and skin health, though its bioavailability is limited.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Small amounts of zinc, iron, and phosphorus are present, contributing to metabolic functions.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full for longer.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Most calories come from saturated fat, so consumption should be moderate.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Many commercial versions are heavily salted, which can raise blood pressure in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Pig meat allergy
items.content: Some people may have an allergic reaction to pork proteins.

items.title: Trans fats from reheating
items.content: Repeated heating of the oil can create trans fats, which are detrimental to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pork rinds can be enjoyed straight from the bag, added to salads, soups, or used as a crunchy topping for low‑carb dishes. Choose varieties without artificial flavorings and with moderate salt levels.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep rinds in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life store them in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation. Discard if they develop a rancid smell or off‑flavor.
